evaluated_on: held-out test set (200 applicants), decision threshold 0.27

thresholds_used.rule: status uses the larger of demographic parity difference and equalized odds difference

attributes.description: Sex, derived from the dataset's 'personal status and sex' field. NOT used by the model.
attributes.interpretation: Approval rate is 44% for 'male' vs 41% for 'female' (gap 3%). The largest gap in error rates between groups is 15%. There is a noticeable disparity that should be investigated before any real use. Note: the actual good-credit rate in the data also differs (71% vs 67%), so part of the gap reflects the historical data.

attributes.description: Age under 25 vs 25 and over. Age IS a model input, so differences can be direct.
attributes.interpretation: Approval rate is 48% for '25 and over' vs 23% for 'under 25' (gap 25%). The largest gap in error rates between groups is 29%. There is a large disparity; this model should not be used for this group without mitigation. Note: the actual good-credit rate in the data also differs (75% vs 51%), so part of the gap reflects the historical data.

attributes.description: Foreign-worker status. NOT used by the model.
attributes.interpretation: Approval rate is 67% for 'not foreign worker' vs 42% for 'foreign worker' (gap 24%). The largest gap in error rates between groups is 26%. There is a large disparity; this model should not be used for this group without mitigation. Note: the actual good-credit rate in the data also differs (83% vs 70%), so part of the gap reflects the historical data.
warnings: Group 'not foreign worker' has only 6 test applicants; its metrics are unreliable.

limitations: The test set has only 200 applicants, so group metrics have wide uncertainty.
Only 37 of 1000 applicants in the whole dataset are not foreign workers; that group is very small.
'Sex' is derived from a combined marital-status/sex field; the code 'female : single' never occurs in the data, so single women cannot be distinguished.
Removing sensitive attributes from the model ('fairness through unawareness') does not remove proxies: features such as job, housing or age can correlate with them.
Passing these thresholds does not prove the model is fair. Different fairness definitions can conflict and no single metric is sufficient.
The data come from one German bank in the 1970s-90s and may not represent any current population.
